basics.title: Phuket dishes to look for
basics.text:
Moo hong: pork belly braised with soy, garlic and lots of black pepper, eaten with rice.
Mee Hokkien: thick yellow noodles fried with pork, seafood and greens in a dark gravy, often with an egg on top.
Mee hoon and mee sua: thin rice noodles and fine wheat noodles, fried or in pork bone soup.
Phuket dim sum: small steamed and fried plates for breakfast, eaten with chilli sauce, from about 05:30.
Khanom jeen: fresh rice noodles with your choice of Southern curry and a table of free herbs and pickles.
Gaeng poo: crab meat curry with betel leaves, poured over thin rice noodles.
Gaeng som (gaeng leung): sour, hot orange fish curry with tamarind and turmeric, no coconut milk.
O tao: taro, egg and small oysters fried together until soft and crisp.
Loba: fried pork offal and tofu with a sweet chilli dip.
O aew: clear fig-seed jelly with shaved ice, red syrup and red beans.
A pong: thin coconut crepes cooked over charcoal.
Roti: flat bread fried on a griddle, with curry for breakfast or with banana and condensed milk as a sweet.
Khanom tom, ang ku and other Peranakan sweets: small rice flour cakes with coconut and palm sugar, sold at markets and dessert shops.
Kopi: Phuket coffee, strong and sweet with condensed milk, served in old coffee shops (kopitiam).

basics.title: How ordering and paying works
basics.text: Thai meals are shared: order one dish per person plus rice, put everything in the middle and say 'khao suay' for plain rice. Ask for 'mai phet' (not spicy) or 'phet nit noi' (a little spicy); Southern curries are very hot by default. Shophouses and markets have no service charge and are often cash only; Thai QR (PromptPay) payment needs a Thai bank app, so bring small notes. Smarter restaurants and hotels write prices with '++', which means 10% service charge plus 7% VAT are added; tipping is not expected at local shops, and 20-100 THB or the coins left on the tray is a kind extra at sit-down places.

basics.title: When places open
basics.text: Phuket Town eats early: dim sum shops open 04:00-06:00 and finish by 11:00, roti and khanom jeen shops run about 06:30-13:00, and many famous noodle shophouses close by 15:00-17:00. Dinner places open 17:00-18:00, and only a few cook after 23:00 (Go Benz to 01:30, Ko Ang Seafood to 23:30, Local Canteen to midnight). Many family shops close one day a week, often Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, and some close on Buddhist holy days, so check the day. Night markets: Sunday Walking Street on Sunday, Naka on Saturday and Sunday, Chillva Monday to Saturday.

basics.title: Pork and halal
basics.text: The Hokkien-Chinese shops of the Old Town cook a lot of pork: moo hong, crispy pork, pork satay, loba and pork lard in the noodles. Muslim shops serve no pork and often no alcohol; you can tell them by a green halal sign or the word 'halal' in Arabic or Thai (ฮาลาล), women staff in headscarves, and menus of beef, chicken and goat curry with roti. In this guide Roti Chaofa and Roti Taew Nam are halal. If you want no pork in a Chinese shop, say 'mai sai moo'.

basics.title: Seafood priced by weight
basics.text: At seafood places fish, crab, lobster and mantis shrimp are often sold by the kilo or by 100 g, and the menu may only say 'market price'. Before they cook, ask the weight and the total price ('kilo la thao rai?'), watch them weigh it, and write the total down. Local places in Phuket Town, Laem Hin and Kathu charge much less than beach restaurants; a 2024 review of one local Phuket seafood restaurant listed fish at 500-600 THB a kilo. Check the bill for items you did not order.
